extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American government; policymakers; informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing how the U.S. House of Representatives conducts legislative business, with emphasis on the role of standing committees, rules that shape debate, transparency, and the opportunities available to individual members. Useful for analyzing institutional design and democratic deliberation in the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the principle that the Committees shall rule without let or hindrance' — Standing Committees consign the entire direction of legislation upon subjects that come to their consideration and 'give shape and course to the determinations of the House.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that committees determine initiation, shape, and opportunities for debate; committees usually control the floor, the sequence of consideration, and can effectively legislate in committee-rooms. Examples: committees framing bills, controlling reporting, and excluding other members' initiative except via referral tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of new members' usefulness by rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and precedents are 'framed for the deliberate purpose of making usefulness unattainable by individual members' — new members find privileges curtailed and must learn customs (e.g., Monday for introductions, referral to committee) to avoid being shut out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes practical obstacles a new member faces: difficulty gaining the floor, requirement of unanimous consent to introduce or discuss a bill on the floor, and routine referral to committees. Use this to evaluate whether institutional rules permit meaningful participation by newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedition of business versus thorough debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The House is 'conscious that time presses' and is 'eager to hurry business,' resulting in practices that limit debate (use of the previous question, strict time allotments, suspension of rules) to expedite legislative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details mechanisms that prioritize speed: reporting committee hour, the move of the previous question that precludes amendments, one-hour chief hour of debate, and the majority's general preference to hurry. Use to judge whether the balance between efficiency and deliberation is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged treatment of certain committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Some committees (notably Ways and Means and Appropriations) are 'specially licensed' and have extraordinary privileges; revenue and supply bills may be reported and considered at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the hierarchy of committee privileges: the four committees (including Printing and Elections) receive preferential access/time; other committees take turns. Use to evaluate fairness and prioritization in agenda-setting and deliberative attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional overlap and referral contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee jurisdictions 'overlap at many points,' producing 'sharp and interesting skirmishes' over commitment of bills when subjects lie within multiple committees' purviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (e.g., railroad fare regulation could go to Commerce or Pacific Railroads; mailing prohibitions might go to Post-Offices or Judiciary). Use to assess clarity of jurisdictional rules and whether overlap enables strategic behavior or obstructs prompt disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death by neglect (committee inaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill 'goes ... to dim dungeons of silence whence it will never return' — committees commonly let bills expire unreported rather than formally reject them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains method: committees substitute their own drafts, fail to report on many bills, and effectively kill measures by inaction. Use as a metric of responsiveness and barriers to legislative success for private members' proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee control of floor debate and amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting committee-man 'is the chief hour of debate' and by undisputed privilege controls who speaks, how long, and whether amendments are in order; he typically moves the previous question to block further amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete procedural description: reporting member retains control, grants time only to those promised beforehand, bars amendments unless consented, and moves the previous question to secure final disposition. Use to evaluate openness of floor deliberation and minority participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee secrecy versus public enlightenment
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings of committees are 'private' and 'their discussions unpublished'; committees are commissioned to 'instruct and guide the House,' not the public, which limits public understanding of legislative reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that committee hearings are not intended for public instruction, are privileged, and that members may be breaching order if they allude on the floor to committee proceedings. Use as a transparency criterion: extent of openness, publication of proceedings, and effect on public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of committee debate (advocacy vs. principled contest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches made before Committees are 'the pleas of special pleaders' and 'could scarcely either inform or elevate public opinion'; they lack 'the searching, critical, illuminating character of the higher order of parliamentary debate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes advocacy-oriented committee hearings from open-floor debates between recognized leaders where principles are contested. Use to evaluate whether deliberation is substantive, balanced, and educative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical and architectural impediments to debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The chamber's architecture — 'spread at large through the vast spaces' with roomy desks, broad aisles, and deep galleries — makes business-like debate and easy interchange of views by the representative body impractical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues environment matters: a large, dispersed chamber discourages close, sympathetic contact and deliberative interchange. Use as an institutional design factor when assessing capacity for collective deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of deliberative function to committees
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Congress, or at any rate the House of Representatives, delegates not only its legislative but also its deliberative functions to its Standing Committees' — the House 'legislates in its committee-rooms' and sits in session mainly to sanction committee conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains consequence: public session is often formal/ceremonial while real work occurs in private committees. Use to judge whether democratic deliberation (visibility, accountability) has been effectively delegated and whether that delegation is legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for public, high-stakes floor discussion for democratic instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: For public instruction there is needed 'a discussion by the sovereign legislative body itself ... in which every feature of each mooted point ... shall be distinctly brought out' and where 'something ... evidently depends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets normative standard: important and high-stakes issues require public, full debate by recognized leaders to inform the public and legitimize decisions. Use to assess whether key matters receive appropriate public deliberation.
